articles.title: Energy, Fertilizer Costs and El Niño Raise Global Food Crisis Risks - Grain Journal
articles.summary: Energy, Fertilizer Costs and El Niño Raise Global Food Crisis Risks  Grain Journal
articles.full_text:
Rising energy and fertilizer costs, resilient biofuel demand and increasing weather risks from a strong El Niño could combine to threaten global food production, according to a report from the S&P Global Institute.
The report, “Energy Disruption and El Niño: Leading to a Global Food Crisis?” examines how disruptions to energy and fertilizer supplies linked to the Iran war could compound agricultural challenges as farmers face higher operating costs and potentially adverse growing conditions. The analysis draws on expertise from S&P Global's agricultural and energy research services and S&P Global Ratings.
The Middle East's role in global fertilizer markets is a significant concern. Before the conflict, about 20% of global oil supplies and 20% of global liquefied natural gas trade moved through the Strait of Hormuz. The waterway is also a critical route for fertilizer and fertilizer feedstocks.
Approximately 29% of global urea trade, nearly half of global sulfur trade and about 21% of merchant ammonia trade normally pass through the strait. Urea is the world's most widely used nitrogen fertilizer.
Disruptions to these supplies threaten fertilizer availability while increasing production costs elsewhere. Fertilizer manufacturers outside the Gulf region depend on energy, particularly natural gas, for both feedstocks and manufacturing. Restrictions on oil and LNG flows therefore can increase fertilizer production costs and farm operating expenses well beyond the immediate conflict zone.
South Asia faces particular exposure because of its reliance on Gulf fertilizer imports and LNG. India imports significant quantities of urea from Gulf producers, while LNG supports about 85% of its domestic urea production. In Bangladesh, LNG shortages have forced four of the country's five urea fertilizer plants to cease operations since March 2026.
Diesel shortages are adding further pressure to farm economics, including in regions less directly affected by fertilizer supply disruptions. The Middle East and Russia typically account for half of global net diesel exports, but supplies from both regions have contracted sharply.
Middle Eastern diesel exports fell by more than half from July 2025 levels to less than 1 million barrels per day in July 2026. Ukrainian drone attacks and an export ban have pushed Russian diesel exports from approximately 1 million barrels per day toward zero. China also has tightened restrictions on diesel and jet fuel exports.
With remaining refining capacity operating near its limits, reduced supplies and low inventories are colliding with seasonal harvest and winter heating demand. The price difference between crude oil and diesel, historically between $12 and $20 per barrel, exceeded $100 per barrel in the first week of September.
Higher diesel prices increase the cost of operating farm machinery and transporting agricultural commodities. Combined with more expensive fertilizer, the increases could force farmers in the most affected regions to reduce fertilizer purchases and application rates or plant fewer acres, ultimately lowering production.
High oil prices also make biofuels more competitive with petroleum-based fuels, supporting demand for the crops and vegetable oils used to produce them. In September 2026, biofuels became cheaper than oil-based shipping fuels in Europe for the first time in recorded history.
Resilient biofuel demand and policy support could limit the ability of crop markets to shift supplies toward food production as input costs rise. The report notes that biofuel policies influence planting decisions at a time when farmers are already weighing higher production expenses.
A potentially strong El Niño could intensify these pressures by exposing crops to heat and disruptive rainfall while higher input costs leave farmers with fewer resources to protect yields. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration projects sea-surface temperatures could reach at least 2 degrees Celsius above normal, a threshold reached only seven times since the 1950s.
S&P Global's agricultural modeling has reduced Brazil's corn production forecast by 6 million metric tons to 137 million metric tons. If El Niño intensifies, output could fall by an additional 10 million metric tons.
Australia's wheat production could decline to 22 million metric tons, compared with the current forecast of 28 million metric tons. India's rabi wheat crop also faces increased downside risk if monsoon rainfall deficits persist. September rainfall was approximately 14% below average.
Brazil's soybean production forecast has been lowered by 6 million metric tons to 177 million metric tons. A model accounting for El Niño severity and reduced phosphate application produces a probability-weighted estimate of 168 million metric tons, with a 65% probability that output falls between 160 million and 170 million metric tons. Lower production could have global consequences because Brazilian soybeans are a major feed source for China's livestock industry.
Palm oil production also faces potential declines, with downside risks estimated at 5.8 million metric tons in Indonesia and 2.5 million metric tons in Malaysia.
The report cautions that the effects on food markets will emerge more slowly than changes in energy prices. Farmers purchase seed, fertilizer and fuel months before selling their crops, meaning the current squeeze on farm budgets may not significantly affect food markets until 2027.
A global food crisis is not inevitable, but the combination of prolonged conflict, disrupted energy and fertilizer supplies, higher production costs and adverse weather could increase the risk. If these pressures persist and harvests decline across several major producing regions, global food supplies could face substantial challenges.
Source: S&P Global, "Out of Hormuz Energy Shocks, the Ingredients for a Global Food Crisis"

articles.title: Cheniere signs 4 MMtpy LNG supply deals with QatarEnergy through 2054 - Pipeline and Gas Journal
articles.summary: Cheniere signs 4 MMtpy LNG supply deals with QatarEnergy through 2054  Pipeline and Gas Journal
articles.full_text:
Cheniere will supply QatarEnergy with 4 MMtpy of LNG from Sabine Pass and Corpus Christi from the early 2030s through 2054, partly tied to an expansion FID.
(P&GJ) — Cheniere Energy has signed long-term agreements to supply QatarEnergy with a total of 4 million metric tons per year (MMtpy) of LNG through 2054, as the company moves to expand production capacity at its Sabine Pass terminal.
Under the agreements, QatarEnergy will buy 2 MMtpy each from Cheniere subsidiaries Sabine Pass Liquefaction in Louisiana and Corpus Christi Liquefaction in Texas on a free-on-board basis. Pricing is indexed to Henry Hub plus a fixed fee. Deliveries are expected to begin in the early 2030s and continue through the end of 2054.
One MMtpy of the Sabine Pass agreement is subject to a positive final investment decision on the first phase of the Sabine Pass expansion project.
"These pivotal, multi-decade agreements with QatarEnergy, one of the world's most important energy companies and a cornerstone of the global LNG industry, represent a major long-term commercial commitment and reinforce Cheniere's position as the leader in U.S. LNG," said Jack Fusco, Cheniere's chairman, president and CEO.
The Sabine Pass expansion, being developed through Cheniere Energy Partners, is expected to add up to about 20 MMtpy of peak production capacity, including estimated debottlenecking, raising the terminal's total capacity to more than 50 MMtpy. Cheniere plans to build the expansion in phases.
The first phase is expected to include a single liquefaction train, Train 7, and a boil-off gas reliquefaction unit, along with supporting infrastructure and tie-ins to the existing terminal, with total capacity of more than 6 MMtpy. Cheniere signed a lump-sum, turnkey engineering, procurement and construction contract with Bechtel Energy for the first phase in May 2026, and Bechtel has begun early engineering and procurement under a limited notice to proceed.
Cheniere operates about 56 MMtpy of liquefaction capacity at Sabine Pass and Corpus Christi, with about 5 MMtpy more under construction.

articles.title: Lithium Nitrate Additive Market To 2035: High-Nickel Battery Demand Supports 8–12% CAGR - News and Statistics - IndexBox
articles.summary: Lithium Nitrate Additive Market To 2035: High-Nickel Battery Demand Supports 8–12% CAGR - News and Statistics  IndexBox
articles.full_text:
Abstract
According to the latest IndexBox report on the global Lithium Nitrate Additive market, the market enters 2026 with broader demand fundamentals, more disciplined procurement behavior, and a more regionally diversified supply architecture.
The global lithium nitrate additive market is entering a phase of accelerated expansion, with demand projected to grow at an 8–12% CAGR between 2026 and 2035. This growth is anchored in the additive's indispensable function as a passivation salt in high-nickel lithium-ion battery cathodes, where it suppresses parasitic side reactions and extends cycle life—a critical performance requirement for electric-vehicle and grid-storage batteries targeting 1,000 or more cycles.
Battery cathode applications already account for 70–80% of global consumption, and this share is expected to rise as cathode makers increasingly qualify lithium nitrate as a standard formulation component for next-generation NCM and NCA chemistries. Beyond batteries, the product retains niche but stable demand in corrosion inhibition, chemical processing, and specialty catalyst formulations. Supply remains highly concentrated, with more than 70% of world production located in China, leaving Europe and North America import-dependent for over 90% of their requirements.
This geographic imbalance, combined with feedstock lithium carbonate price volatility and regulatory fragmentation across REACH, TSCA, and CNCA frameworks, shapes both the opportunities and the risks in the outlook. The report provides a data-driven view of market size, demand architecture, supply structure, trade flows, pricing logic, and competitive positioning through 2035.
The baseline scenario for the lithium nitrate additive market assumes continued expansion of high-nickel cathode production, steady qualification of the additive in battery gigafactory supply chains, and gradual diversification of supply away from a single-country concentration. Under this scenario, global demand advances at an 8–12% CAGR from 2026 to 2035, with the market index rising from 100 in 2025 to approximately 240 by 2035. Battery cathode applications remain the principal engine, supported by multi-year volume agreements replacing spot purchases as cathode makers lock in supply for gigafactory ramps.
High-purity and specialty-formulated grades (≥99.5% purity) grow faster than standard industrial grades, commanding premium pricing 20–40% above standard and lifting the overall value pool. Specialty industrial uses—corrosion inhibitors, chemical processing, and stabilisers—provide a stable but slower-growing base. On the supply side, China's dominant production position persists through the forecast horizon, though capacity additions in Europe, North America, and select Asia-Pacific locations gradually reduce import dependence.
Feedstock lithium carbonate price volatility remains the key margin risk, with fluctuations of 3–4× over the past two years discouraging long-term investment outside established supply chains. Regulatory compliance costs, adding 5–15% to delivered cost for cross-border shipments, disproportionately affect smaller importers. The baseline does not assume a demand collapse in battery chemistries; rather, it assumes continued mix shift toward high-nickel formulations where lithium nitrate's passivation function is most valued.
Demand Drivers and Constraints
Primary Demand Drivers
- Essential passivation function in high-nickel NCM and NCA battery cathodes, extending cycle life beyond 1,000 cycles and supporting EV and grid-storage performance requirements.
- Rapid capacity expansion of battery gigafactories, which are shifting from spot purchases to annual volume agreements and embedding lithium nitrate as a standard formulation component.
- Rising demand for high-purity and specialty-formulated grades (≥99.5% purity) as cathode makers tighten quality specifications, with premium pricing 20–40% above standard grades.
- Growth in grid-scale energy storage deployments, which require long-cycle-life batteries and reinforce cathode additive demand.
- Qualification of lithium nitrate in next-generation cathode chemistries by major battery-cell manufacturers, raising volume purchase commitments.
- Import dependence of Europe and North America—over 90% of supply—prompting regional sourcing initiatives and long-term contracts that support market formalization.
Potential Growth Constraints
- Feedstock lithium carbonate price volatility, with fluctuations of 3–4× over the past two years, erodes additive producer margins and discourages long-term investment outside China.
- Geographic concentration of production in China creates supply-chain risk for European and North American buyers, who face 8–16 week lead times and reliance on a limited number of qualified suppliers.
- Regulatory fragmentation across REACH in Europe, TSCA in the US, and CNCA in China adds 5–15% to delivered cost for cross-border shipments, particularly for smaller importers.
- Qualification cycles for battery-grade additives are lengthy, slowing adoption by new cathode makers and limiting near-term demand diversification.
- Potential substitution or reformulation of cathode chemistries that reduce or eliminate the need for passivation additives in certain battery designs.
Demand Structure by End-Use Industry
End-Use Industry Demand Split (%)
Battery cathode materials (NCM/NCA) (estimated share: 75%)
Battery cathode materials represent the dominant and fastest-growing outlet for lithium nitrate additive, accounting for roughly three-quarters of global consumption. The additive functions as a passivation salt in high-nickel cathode slurries, forming a stable surface film on cathode particles that suppresses parasitic side reactions and extends cell cycle life—a critical requirement for electric-vehicle and grid-storage batteries targeting 1,000 or more cycles. Demand-side indicators to watch include gigafactory capacity announcements, high-nickel cathode mix ratios, and the pace of qualification by major cell manufacturers.
Through 2035, cathode makers are expected to shift from spot purchases to annual volume agreements, embedding lithium nitrate as a standard formulation component. Growth is reinforced by the mix shift toward NCM and NCA chemistries with higher nickel content, where passivation is most valuable. High-purity grades (≥99.5%) are gaining share within this segment, commanding premium pricing 20–40% above standard grades as cathode makers tighten specifications. Current trend: Rising.
Major trends: Shift from spot to annual volume agreements as gigafactories seek price stability, Rising qualification of lithium nitrate as a standard formulation component, Mix shift toward high-nickel NCM and NCA cathodes, Growing demand for high-purity grades (≥99.5%) with premium pricing, and Expansion of grid-storage battery production reinforcing long-cycle-life requirements.
Representative participants: Albemarle Corporation, Ganfeng Lithium, Tianqi Lithium, Livent Corporation, and SQM.
Industrial chemical processing (estimated share: 10%)
Industrial chemical processing uses lithium nitrate additive as a specialty reagent and processing aid in various chemical manufacturing operations, including catalyst formulations and intermediate synthesis. Demand in this segment is relatively stable and tied to broader industrial production cycles rather than battery megatrends. Buyers are typically chemical-processing firms and toll manufacturers that require consistent specification grades, often standard industrial purity rather than battery-grade. Through 2035, growth is expected to track GDP-linked industrial output, with modest gains from process intensification and specialty chemical expansion.
Demand-side indicators include chemical production indices, capacity utilization rates in process industries, and the pace of new specialty chemical plant construction. The segment is less sensitive to lithium carbonate price volatility than battery applications because volumes are smaller and procurement is often contract-based. However, regulatory compliance costs for cross-border shipments affect smaller importers disproportionately, which can constrain segment growth in import-dependent regions. Current trend: Stable.
Major trends: Stable demand tied to industrial production cycles, Modest growth from specialty chemical expansion, Contract-based procurement insulating volumes from spot price volatility, Regulatory compliance costs affecting smaller importers, and Process intensification supporting consistent additive consumption.
Representative participants: Thermo Fisher Scientific, Merck KGaA, Honeywell International, and American Elements.
Corrosion inhibition (estimated share: 8%)
Corrosion inhibition represents a niche but durable application for lithium nitrate additive, particularly in closed-loop cooling systems, industrial water treatment, and metal protection formulations. The additive's mechanism involves forming a protective film on metal surfaces that reduces oxidation and extends equipment life. Demand is driven by maintenance, repair, and operations spending across process industries, power generation, and HVAC systems. Through 2035, growth is expected to be modest and steady, supported by aging industrial infrastructure in developed markets and new plant construction in emerging economies. Demand-side indicators include industrial capex, maintenance spending, and water-treatment chemical consumption.
The segment is less cyclical than battery applications but also offers limited upside. Suppliers typically serve this market through distributors and specialty chemical formulators, with standard grades dominating. Regulatory shifts toward environmentally benign corrosion inhibitors could create substitution risk, but lithium nitrate's performance characteristics maintain its position in critical applications. articles.title: Kinder Morgan takes FID on Southeast Connector, Permian Link natural gas pipelines - Oil & Gas Journal
articles.summary: Kinder Morgan takes FID on Southeast Connector, Permian Link natural gas pipelines  Oil & Gas Journal
articles.full_text:
Kinder Morgan Inc. (KMI) has taken final investment decision (FID) on its Southeast Connector and Permian Link natural gas pipeline projects. Southern Natural Gas (SNG), a KMI subsidiary, secured sufficient long-term, take-or-pay transportation agreements with shippers to proceed with Southeast Connector, designed to transport up to 2.6 bcfd through about 470 miles of new pipeline.
Subject to receipt of required permits and approvals, service is expected to begin in phases starting fourth-quarter 2030. The $3.1-billion project could be expanded if demand warrants.
“Large-load interconnection requests across the Southeast now exceed 200 Gw,” said KMI chief executive officer and director Kimberly Dang in the company’s earnings call, noting that this could represent roughly 8 bcfd of natural gas demand if it all came to fruition and if it was all served by gas-fired generation.
Natural Gas Pipeline Co. of America (NGPL), another KMI subsidiary, reached FID on the 2.8-bcfd Permian Link. Estimated cost of the project is $4.2-billion, of which KMI's share is expected to be about $1.6 billion.
The 434-mile pipeline will serve new power generation for an A-rated hyperscaler and is supported by long-term, take-or-pay transportation agreements. NGPL expects to place the project in service third-quarter 2030, subject to required permits and approvals.
KMI also sanctioned the second and third phases of its Creekside Lateral project in central Texas, following execution of additional long-term, take-or-pay agreements with data center and industrial customers. The company has now contracted 750 MMcfd of the system’s 1.3-bcfd design capacity, with potential for future expansion to more than 2 bcfd. KMI expects to place the project in service in phases, beginning fourth-quarter 2026 and continuing throught fourth-quarter 2027, subject to permits and approvals.
SNG and Tennessee Gas Pipeline (TGP), meanwhile, took FID on the 10-bcf Bear Creek Storage Expansion project, to be used by TGP which has secured long-term binding agreements for the capacity. The extra capacity is expected to enter service in April 2029, subject to required permits and approvals.
Refined products, terminals
KMI's Houston Ship Channel refined products hub moved 427,000 b/d across its 11 docks in third-quarter 2026, a 39% year-on-year increase and an all-time record for the site. The company attributed the record quarter to the worldwide shortage in refined product supplies and associated price dislocations and is advancing enhancements to in-tank blending capabilities for butane and other gasoline components.
Permitting and right-of-way acquisition also are progressing for two dedicated refined products pipelines connecting KMI's Pasadena Terminal with a nearby major refinery. The $139-million project is backed by a long-term storage and volume commitment with a major national oil company and is expected to enter service third-quarter 2027.
KMI is also expanding its 1.5-million-bbl Kinder Morgan Export Terminal on the Houston Ship Channel. The $30-million project is supported by a long-term storage commitment with a major international trading company and is expected to be placed in service first-quarter 2027.
Earnings
The announcements and project updates were part of KMI’s third-quarter 2026 earnings reporting. The company reported net income attributable to KMI of $764 million, up nearly 22% from third-quarter 2025.
The power sector is investing at record levels. The lesson holds for any energy operator: building the asset is the visible half. Getting it to run through every handover in its lifecycle decides whether the investment performs.
Chris joined Oil & Gas Journal in 2005 as Pipeline Editor, having already worked for more than a decade in a variety of oil and gas industry analysis and reporting roles. He became editor-in-chief in 2019 and head of content in 2025.

articles.title: AI’s Hidden Supply Chain: The Critical Minerals Behind the Intelligence Boom - trendsgroup.org
articles.summary: AI’s Hidden Supply Chain: The Critical Minerals Behind the Intelligence Boom  trendsgroup.org
articles.full_text:
As artificial intelligence (AI) advances from an experimental technology into a foundational layer of the global economy, attention has focused largely on its most visible physical constraints: electricity, data center capacity, and water for cooling. Yet the more consequential bottleneck may lie further upstream, in the minerals required to manufacture the semiconductors, power systems, transmission equipment, cooling infrastructure, and energy-storage technologies on which the AI economy depends.
These minerals are becoming increasingly vulnerable to supply-chain disruption for two interconnected reasons. First, AI is adding demand to materials already under pressure from other fast-growing industries, including electric vehicles, renewable energy, and semiconductor manufacturing. Second, the mining, refining and processing of these materials remain concentrated in a relatively small number of countries, leaving manufacturers and technology companies exposed to potential disruptions. China, for example, is the leading refiner for 19 of the 20 strategic minerals tracked by the International Energy Agency (IEA), with an average market share of around 70%.[1]
The emerging challenge is therefore larger than securing enough GPUs. The next phase of the AI race will be decided not only in chip-design labs and hyperscale data centers, but also in mines, refineries, power plants, and transmission corridors. Scaling AI increasingly depends on whether economies can build the physical infrastructure around compute and secure the copper, aluminum, gallium, germanium, rare earths and other materials needed to deliver it at speed.
This article explores: (i) how AI infrastructure is creating new sources of demand across critical mineral supply chains, (ii) where emerging bottlenecks and geographic concentrations could expose AI expansion to supply risks, (iii) how governments are responding through critical mineral strategies, export controls, domestic production, and supply-chain diversification, and (iv) how technology, mining, and infrastructure companies are adapting their investments. Together, these developments could make access to critical materials an increasingly important dimension of global AI competition.
Mapping AI’s material dependencies
As AI infrastructure expands, demand is rising not only for the specialized materials used in advanced electronics, but also for the industrial metals required to connect, power and cool these systems. The minerals underpinning that architecture can therefore be grouped into two broad categories: those needed directly for computing and communications, and those needed indirectly to build and operate the infrastructure that supports them. Directly needed minerals, including gallium and germanium, are used in semiconductors, high-performance electronics and fiber-optic communications. Gallium is used in compound semiconductors and high-performance power electronics, technologies that can operate at higher frequencies, temperatures, and voltages than conventional silicon-based components. Rare earth elements support the permanent magnets found in motors, cooling equipment, and other electrical systems used throughout data center infrastructure.
Indirectly needed minerals, most notably copper and aluminum, form the backbone of the power, cooling, transmission, and data center infrastructure that enables AI to operate at scale. Copper is the clearest example of how AI’s material footprint extends far beyond the server rack. Inside a data center, copper is used in cabling, busbars, power-distribution systems, cooling equipment, and electrical connections. Aluminum plays a similar role. Its lower weight and strong conductivity make it essential to transmission networks and electrical equipment, while its use in data center structures, heat-management systems and cooling infrastructure gives it a direct connection to the physical expansion of computing capacity.
Outside the facility, the requirements become even more substantial. Large-scale computing projects can require new substations, transformers, transmission lines, distribution upgrades, and dedicated generation capacity. In other words, AI does not merely consume electricity. It consumes the infrastructure required to deliver reliable electricity at scale. That distinction is becoming increasingly important as data centers grow larger and more concentrated. A single hyperscale campus can represent a major new industrial load, forcing utilities and developers to accelerate grid connections and expand equipment capacity. Every additional layer from the transmission network to the facility’s internal power systems adds to the demand for copper. While directly needed materials may be consumed in relatively small quantities compared with copper or aluminum, their strategic importance comes from the difficulty to substitute. These are often produced as by-products and processed through highly concentrated supply chains. A small physical requirement can therefore create a large commercial vulnerability if access is disrupted.
There is also another layer of indirect materials becoming increasingly relevant to AI data centers, and these are lithium, graphite and nickel. They enter the AI supply chain through a different route, namely energy storage. Data centers require uninterrupted power. As their electricity demand rises, operators and utilities are deploying larger battery systems to provide backup power, manage short-duration fluctuations, and support the integration of renewable energy. Batteries can also help reduce pressure on constrained grids by shifting electricity use or providing fast-response capacity during periods of peak demand. That makes AI infrastructure an indirect but increasingly important source of demand for battery materials. The connection is particularly significant in markets where data center developers are pursuing renewable power commitments or where grid reliability is insufficient to support rapid expansion without additional storage.
However, AI is unlikely to become the largest source of global demand for every material it touches. Electric vehicles, renewable energy systems, electricity networks, and battery storage remain larger consumers of several critical minerals. But AI is arriving at a moment when those sectors are already competing for the same supplies. Global lithium demand increased by almost 30% in 2024, while demand for nickel, cobalt, graphite, and rare earth elements rose by between 6% and 8%, according to the IEA.[2] Much of that growth was driven by electric vehicles, battery storage, renewable energy and grid investment. Therefore, the significance of AI lies less in its share of total mineral demand than in the timing, location, and concentration of the demand it adds and is considered a powerful new competitor.
The geography problem: location of minerals is only half the story
The countries leading the AI race are not necessarily the countries controlling the materials that make it possible. The United States dominates much of the AI software stack. American companies design the leading chips, build the largest cloud platforms, and are investing billions of dollars in new data centers. Europe is trying to secure a role in advanced computing and industrial AI. China is pursuing technological self-sufficiency at national scale.
But the physical supply chain behind that competition follows a very different map. Copper comes primarily from Chile, Peru, and the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC). Australia, Chile, China, and Argentina are central to the lithium supply. Guinea is a critical source of bauxite, the ore used to produce aluminum. DRC supplies most of the world’s mined cobalt.[3] Those countries may not control the AI platforms being built in Silicon Valley, Seattle, Beijing, or Paris. They control the raw materials without which the servers, power systems, batteries, transmission networks, and cooling equipment cannot be manufactured.
Even that description, however, is incomplete. Mining is only the first stage of the supply chain and often not the stage where the greatest strategic power resides. The decisive bottleneck is frequently found later, in refining, chemical conversion, separation, component manufacturing, and the production of materials that meet industrial specifications. A country may have the ore, but another country may control the technology, facilities, and commercial relationships needed to turn that ore into a usable input.
China has spent decades building precisely this kind of downstream capacity. Its influence is therefore much greater than its share of mining alone would suggest. In magnet rare earths, China accounted for roughly 60% of global mining in 2024, but about 91% of separation and refining and 94% of sintered permanent-magnet production, according to the IEA.[4]
That progression from mine to refinery to finished component is the real story. The material that leaves a mine is rarely the material purchased by a semiconductor manufacturer, battery producer, or data center equipment supplier. Between the two are processing plants, specialized chemical facilities, logistics networks, technical expertise, and years of accumulated industrial know-how. Recreating that system is expensive, slow, and often environmentally contentious. Gallium demonstrates why this matters for AI. It is not typically extracted from dedicated mines. Instead, it is recovered as a by-product of processing bauxite and zinc ores. Germanium is similarly tied to the processing of other mineral streams. If prices rise, producers cannot simply decide to open a new gallium or germanium mine. Supply depends on the economics and capacity of much larger industries and on whether the relevant refining infrastructure exists outside China.

articles.title: Critical minerals: The missing link in India’s green push - BizzBuzz
articles.summary: Critical minerals: The missing link in India’s green push  BizzBuzz
articles.full_text:
India’s transition to Net Zero depends on a resilient critical minerals supply chain.
India’s clean energy transition will depend not just on how much renewable power it generates, but also on whether it can secure the minerals needed to build that future. Lithium, cobalt, nickel, graphite, copper and rare earth elements are becoming strategic assets as electric mobility, battery manufacturing and renewable energy expand.
Yet, with demand for critical minerals projected to rise four to ten times by 2047, India faces a challenge that extends well beyond mining: building a resilient domestic ecosystem that can withstand global supply disruptions.
A recent Grant Thornton report estimates that electric vehicle battery demand alone could reach 110–130 GWh by 2030. Meeting this requirement, alongside India’s target of 500 GW of non-fossil fuel capacity by the same year, will intensify pressure on mineral supplies.
The ambition to achieve Net Zero emissions by 2070 makes the task even more urgent. Excessive dependence on imported minerals and processed materials could expose Indian industry to geopolitical tensions, volatile prices and export restrictions.
The National Critical Mineral Mission (NCMM), backed by an outlay of Rs34,300 crore, is an important step towards addressing these vulnerabilities.
But policy intent must translate into capabilities across the entire value chain, from exploration and extraction to refining, separation, recycling and advanced manufacturing. Mining alone will not deliver strategic autonomy if higher-value processing remains concentrated overseas.
Financing is a crucial missing link. Critical mineral projects, particularly refining and recycling facilities, require substantial capital, involve technological risks and often take years to become commercially viable. Grant Thornton recommends a diversified financing architecture involving sovereign green bonds, fiscal incentives, foreign direct investment, venture capital, bank lending supported by guarantees and multilateral funding.
India should also consider a dedicated sovereign critical minerals fund, drawing lessons from countries such as Canada, to support strategically important projects that private capital may initially find unattractive. Equally important is the opportunity presented by recycling. According to UN Trade and Development (UNCTAD), the global market for recycled critical minerals could expand from nearly $40 billion in 2020 to $200 billion by 2050.
India should seize this opportunity by developing systems for collecting, recovering and reprocessing materials from used batteries, electronic waste and industrial scrap. A domestic recycling economy potentially worth $10–15 billion annually would reduce import dependence, conserve resources and create new industrial capabilities. Recycling, however, requires clear standards, predictable regulations and investment in collection and processing infrastructure.
Domestic capacity must be complemented by strategic overseas partnerships. India cannot assume that its geological resources alone will satisfy future demand. Government-to-government agreements, long-term offtake contracts, public-private partnerships with global miners and investments in overseas mining and processing assets can diversify supply. Trade policy, too, must be deployed strategically to secure access while encouraging domestic value addition.
As Rabin Roy, founder-managing director of ScholarLab Foundation, points out, the challenge is not merely rising demand, but also who controls processing and captures economic value. Mineral-rich developing economies risk remaining exporters of raw materials while others reap the gains from processing and manufacturing.
Finally, fragmented policymaking must give way to coordinated execution. The Ministries of Mines, Finance, Environment, Commerce, External Affairs, Power and New and Renewable Energy, among others, need a common strategic framework. Environmental safeguards and community interests must remain integral to faster project development.
India’s critical minerals strategy should be judged not by the tonnes it extracts, but by the value it creates, the supply risks it reduces and the industries it builds. Strategic self-reliance will require capital, technological depth and global partnerships.
The race for critical minerals is ultimately a race to secure the foundations of India’s clean energy and industrial future.

articles.full_text:
During his visit to Sydney and Melbourne, the Minister will participate in various programmes and hold extensive discussions with government representatives, mining companies, research institutions and industry leaders from Australia and other countries.
The key objective of the visit is to strengthen critical mineral supply chains to meet India's growing industrial and clean energy requirements and explore opportunities to diversify sources of mineral supplies.

articles.title: Report: Ingredients in place for global food crisis - World Grain

articles.full_text:
NEW YORK, NEW YORK, US – Shortages of fertilizer and fuel combined with the effects of El Niño could lead to a global food crisis in 2027, according to a report released by S&P Global.
The war between the United States and Iran, which began Feb. 28, has resulted in a drastic reduction in shipping traffic along the Strait of Hormuz, a critical international waterway located in the Middle East. About 20% of the world’s global oil and liquified natural gas (LNG) supplies were moved through the waterway before the war, and an even larger percentage of fertilizer typically passes through the strait.
The authors of the report, released on Oct. 19, noted that the reinforcing shocks of higher energy and fertilizer costs, resilient biofuel-linked demand and El Niño-related weather risk are starting to emerge.
“Farmers buy seed, fertilizer and fuel months before they sell a crop,” the authors said. “The squeeze now bearing down on farm budgets may therefore not reach food markets in force until 2027.”
About 30% of urea — the world’s most widely used nitrogen fertilizer — traded on the global market passes through the Strait of Hormuz, as does about half of the global sulfur trade and 21% of ammonia.
Yet, the fertilizer disruption is only the first channel through which the Iran war reaches global agriculture, the authors said. Fertilizer producers elsewhere depend on energy, mainly natural gas, for feedstock as well as fuel for their manufacture. By restricting oil and LNG flows through the Strait of Hormuz, which links the Persian Gulf and the Gulf of Oman, the conflict also raises fertilizer production costs and farm operating costs far beyond the Gulf region.
South Asia is particularly exposed to a double vulnerability of disrupted fertilizer supply from the Gulf and higher costs for the LNG used by domestic producers, the authors note. The Gulf producers are an important source of imported urea for India, while LNG supports around 85% of its domestic urea production. In Bangladesh, the lack of available LNG has resulted in four of the country’s five urea fertilizer plants ceasing operation since March.
The global squeeze on diesel — a key operating cost for farmers — extends to those regions that may otherwise be better insulated from immediate fertilizer and LNG shocks.
The ongoing conflict between Russia and Ukraine, about to enter its fifth year, also has impacted the fertilizer and fuel situation, the report noted. The Middle East and Russia normally account for half of global net diesel exports. Middle Eastern diesel exports have fallen by more than half since July 2025 to less than 1 million barrels per day in July 2026. Meanwhile, Ukrainian drone attacks and an export ban have pushed Russian diesel exports from roughly 1 million barrels per day toward zero. China has tightened its restrictions on exports of diesel and jet fuel, also.
With remaining refining capacity already operating near operational limits, diminished supply and low inventories coinciding with seasonal harvest and winter heating demand has taken its toll. The price differential between a barrel of crude oil and a barrel of diesel (historically between $12 and $20) rose above $100 per barrel in the first week of September.
“The conflict has driven diesel prices up much faster than crude oil prices, exposing farmers to a sharp increase in operating costs,” the authors said. “Faced with this increase, on top of more expensive fertilizer, farmers in the most affected regions either have to reduce fertilizer purchases and the rate at which they apply fertilizer to their crops, or they may choose to reduce the acreage that they plant. Either way, less food would be produced than would otherwise have happened.”
High oil prices also make biofuels more competitive with petroleum, which strengthens demand for the crops and vegetable oils used to produce them. For the first time in recorded history, biofuels became cheaper than oil-based shipping fuels in Europe in September. The resilient demand and policy support for biofuels means that crop markets have less scope to rebalance toward food production.
“Biofuel policy is thus doing more than supporting demand,” the authors said. “It is influencing what farmers plant in the middle of an input-cost shock,” the authors said.
The anticipated strong El Niño would add further stress just as farmers face higher fertilizer and fuel costs, leaving crops less resilient to heat and disruptive rainfall. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration projects sea-surface temperatures to reach at least 2 degrees C above normal — a threshold reached in only seven episodes since the 1950s.
S&P Global’s agriculture modeling now indicates:
- Brazil’s corn output forecast has been reduced by 6 million tonnes, to 137 million tonnes, with a further decline of 10 million tonnes possible if El Niño intensifies.
- Australia’s wheat production could fall to 22 million tonnes, compared with the current forecast of 28 million tonnes.
- India’s rabi wheat crop faces increased downside risk if monsoon deficits persist. September rainfall was approximately 14% below average.
- Brazil’s soybean output forecast has been lowered by 6 million tonnes, to 177 million tonnes. A model incorporating El Niño severity and reduced phosphate application produces a probability-weighted estimate of 168 million tonnes, with a 65% probability that output falls between 160 million and 170 million tonnes. The effects will be felt globally as is China’s largest supplier of soybeans.
Not mentioned in the report but also having a potential impact on food insecurity is the Russia-Ukraine war, which is being waged between two of the world’s largest grain producers and exporters. Attacks on Black Sea shipping lanes, infrastructure destruction, and export disruptions have kept commodity markets volatile, driving the FAO Food Price Index higher and hitting import-dependent nations in North Africa, the Middle East, and parts of Asia hardest.
“Recent escalation in the Russia-Ukraine war has halted the Black Sea grain trade and metastasized into a war on the global food system,” the Council on Foreign Relations said in a report released in September.
The S&P report noted that low-income countries, where food costs amount to about half of the household spending, are especially at risk for an increase in food insecurity in the coming year. While the authors stopped short of saying a global food crisis was inevitable, they say the ingredients for such a catastrophic event are present.
“A global food crisis is not foreordained, but neither is it any longer a distant risk,” the authors said. “If war continues to impede the movement of energy and fertilizer, and if weather cuts harvests across several major producing regions, the elements of such a crisis will be falling into place.”

KEY TAKEAWAYS
• The key to rare earth dominance lies not in which country holds the most patents in a particular field, but in which has the institutional capacity to efficiently translate research and intellectual property into large-scale production that meets industry standards, an area in which China remains the leader.
• Although China has the world’s most comprehensive institutional support for the rare earth industry, China’s rare earth export controls may create additional commercial costs on domestic rare earth firms, increasing pressure on the Chinese government to reconcile firms’ business interests with its geostrategic objectives.
COMMENTARY
China’s rare earth export controls have emerged as a powerful tool in its geopolitical competition with the United States, posing significant risks to the US defence industry, from F-35 fighter jets and Tomahawk missiles to drones. Nevertheless, a widely cited study by Chinese researchers published in mid-2026 has led to an emerging narrative that the geopolitical power of China’s rare earth export controls is declining, with Japan maintaining an overall technological lead in permanent magnets and the United States leading in most core technologies for catalytic, luminescent and polishing materials. Does this signal a crack in China’s rare earth empire? To what extent could it constrain Beijing’s position?
High-Value Patents Do Not Break China’s Empire
China dominates the rare earth industry: with the world’s largest domestic rare earth reserves, it controlled almost 60% of global mining of heavy rare earths in 2024. These elements are essential for the production of high-temperature permanent magnets, which are widely used in advanced defence systems. China also accounted for around 91% of global refining capacity and 94% of global magnet production. Yet the Chinese study has sparked scepticism about China’s ability to translate its strength in supplying rare earth raw materials into leadership in the higher-value technologies built on them.
Despite China filing nearly 26,000 rare earth-related patents between 1950 and 2019, Japan and the United States currently retain leadership in selected foundational downstream technologies. With downstream products accounting for more than 80% of rare earth-related patents worldwide and representing the industry’s most commercially important applications, this raises particular concerns about China’s future leadership in downstream products such as permanent magnets, catalysts, luminescent materials and polishing materials, which shape China’s strategic and economic position in the rare earth industry.
However, the United States and its allies would be heading in the wrong direction if they treat patents as the decisive factor in the rare earth competition. Patent leadership in a particular field is insufficient without the institutional capacity to translate research and intellectual property into commercially viable products that meet industry standards and can be manufactured efficiently at scale. China remains the clear leader in this respect.
China’s Invisible Infrastructure
China’s rare earth dominance is often attributed to its vast reserves and refining capacity. However, these factors explain how China could dominate, rather than why it has been able to sustain that position for decades. The answer lies in a less visible form of infrastructure: a network of universities, state laboratories and industrial policy institutions that links technological discovery to industrial application. Over time, this system has accumulated expertise, institutional knowledge and operational efficiency that reinforce China’s advantage.
For instance, despite the prevailing emphasis in the media on Chinese scientist Xu Guangxian’s counter-current extraction process in the 1970s and its significant contribution to improving rare earth separation, this breakthrough alone did not establish China’s dominance. With light rare earths concentrated mainly in China’s north and heavy rare earths more prevalent in the south, differences in ore characteristics and operating conditions require translating Xu’s innovation into region-specific processing technologies. Two institutions made this possible: the Baotou Research Institute of Rare Earths in the north and the China General Research Institute for Nonferrous Metals in the south. China’s advantage, in other words, was never just the technology. It was the institutional architecture built to regionalise and industrialise it.
That architecture also reproduced itself across generations, making Beijing’s control over refined products less a matter of geology than of workforce pipeline. Xu’s intellectual descendants at Peking University did not simply preserve his methods; they built upon his innovations, developing new adaptations suited to the distinct requirements of northern and southern China. This process has since been institutionalised at scale: a Reuters investigation identified more than 40 specialised rare earth laboratories in China. It also found that at least 11 universities and technical colleges offer rare-earth-related degree programmes, with a combined annual intake of more than 500 students.
In contrast, US efforts have focused largely on mobilising capital and building alliances. In early 2026, the American mining and manufacturing company USA Rare Earth announced a letter of intent with the US Department of Commerce’s CHIPS Program (an initiative to boost the US semiconductor supply chain) that provides for up to $1.3 billion in a senior secured loan and up to $277 million in proposed federal funding. The United States also launched the Forum on Resource Geostrategic Engagement (FORGE) in February 2026, bringing together 55 economies to reduce reliance on Chinese critical mineral supplies.
However, the United States remains constrained by a significant education gap in developing an integrated link between technological research, specialised workforce development and industrial-scale production. Enrolment in undergraduate mining engineering programmes fell from 1,449 in 2015 to 590 in 2023. The number of bachelor’s degrees awarded also fell from 371 to 162 over the same period.
Capital can accelerate project development, but it cannot replace specialised technical judgement. Financing teams without sector-specific knowledge may misprice project risks, while government agencies lacking specialised personnel may delay approvals or fail to identify technical bottlenecks. Furthermore, the international alliances led by the United States may generate diplomatic alignment, but they cannot prevent technical misjudgements, such as misreading mineralogy due to insufficient expertise or producing overly optimistic estimates of recovery rates because of limited processing capacity.
Where Is the Crack?
China’s institutional advantage is strong, but coordination within the system can be difficult. The interests of institutional actors do not always align, creating internal conflicts that can complicate the implementation of central directives. China has undertaken several rounds of consolidation to reduce industry fragmentation. For instance, to raise efficiency, China merged three state-owned enterprises (SOEs) to form China Rare Earth Group in 2021, which controls 62% of national heavy rare earth supplies. However, smuggling persists, opening black market channels that bypass official quotas and potentially reducing China’s bargaining power in trade negotiations.
Additionally, China’s rare earth export controls have placed significant pressure on its mining companies, which are often profit-driven but now face constrained sales. For instance, Chinese exports of rare earth magnets plunged by 75% in the two months following Beijing’s April 2025 export restrictions. Even the state-backed Baotou Rare Earth Products Exchange warned that the resulting damage would not be quickly reversed and described the impact on domestic magnet producers as a “crisis”.
International attention is increasingly focused on November 2026, when China’s current suspension of certain export controls to the United States is due to expire and the measures likely to be reinstated or revised. In the future, China is likely to face a paradox if it continues to use export controls to obtain favourable geostrategic outcomes: the more China relies on export controls, the more commercially costly internal coordination may become. The longer-term international competition over rare earth may hinge on whether China can keep its established system working efficiently, and whether the United States and its allies can build alternatives that endure beyond the current investment push.

articles.title: Springbok lithium project draws US$60m funding offer - MiningMX
articles.summary: Springbok lithium project draws US$60m funding offer  MiningMX
articles.full_text:
DEVELOPING a new lithium mine in a volatile market has obvious risks for lenders, but exploration company Lithium Africa says its Springbok project has attracted two funding offers as it targets first production in 2027.
One is a prepayment and offtake proposal from a “major international commodity trading house”, which would take all of Springbok’s spodumene concentrate for its first three years. The other is a $60m investment proposal from a lithium processing company backed by a Fortune Global 500 group.
Lithium Africa is a Canadian-listed lithium exploration and development company building a portfolio of hard-rock lithium assets across Africa. The Springbok project, in the Northern Cape, sits outside its 50:50 joint venture with GFL International, an affiliate of China’s Ganfeng Lithium.
CEO Thomas Benson said the approaches showed the level of interest in Springbok, describing it as “a permitted mine with a path to production in 2027”.
Under the prepayment proposal, the commodity trader would provide upfront funding in return for 100% of Springbok’s spodumene concentrate for the first three years of production.
Benson told Miningmx discussions over the size of the facility were continuing, but said the prepayment and offtake arrangement was expected to support near-term production.
The second proposal would see the lithium processing company invest $60m in a new holding company containing Lithium Africa’s 70% stake in Namli Exploration & Mining, the South African company that owns Springbok.
The investor would take 55% of the holding company, reducing Lithium Africa’s effective interest in Namli from 70% to 31.5%. Its B-BBEE partner would retain its existing 30%.
Of the $60m, about $10m would go towards drilling across the wider Springbok district and $50m towards a processing plant.
Benson said Lithium Africa’s task was now to select “the partner and the structure that deliver the most value” to shareholders.
The strategy is to get a relatively small operation into production first and use the cash it generates to fund further exploration across the district.
The operation is expected to process existing stockpiled material and newly mined ore through an on-site dense media separation plant to produce spodumene concentrate.
Lithium Africa has not yet disclosed the planned production rate or development cost, saying these should be set out in a preliminary economic assessment in the first half of 2027.
The $60m proposal implies a pre-money valuation of about $70m for 100% of Namli, despite Springbok not yet having a published mineral resource. Lithium Africa told Miningmx the valuation reflected the potential investor’s commercial assessment of the project.
Both offers remain non-binding. The company is also in discussions with about 20 other counterparties over offtake, prepayment, vendor finance and project-level equity. “With more than 20 counterparties engaged, we are running a competitive process,” Benson said.
Several hurdles remain before production. Infill drilling is due to be completed in the first quarter of 2027, followed by an initial mineral resource estimate and preliminary economic assessment in the first half.
Environmental authorisation and a project financing decision are also targeted for that period, with construction planned to start around mid-year.
Lithium outlook
The financing interest comes against a lithium market that remains volatile after a steep price downturn.
Sibanye-Stillwater, which is developing the Keliber lithium project in Finland, said at its interim results in September that lithium hydroxide prices had climbed to almost $28,000/t in May as supply tightened, before retreating as exports resumed from Zimbabwe and expectations of mine restarts elsewhere increased.
Sibanye said demand continued to grow from electric vehicles and energy storage, although new supply was likely to have an impact on prices in the near term. It identified macroeconomic conditions and geopolitical uncertainty as the main downside risks.
The longer-term picture remains one of sharply rising demand. Benchmark Mineral Intelligence – a battery supply-chain research group – estimates global lithium demand will increase from 2.11 million tons (Mt) of lithium carbonate equivalent in 2026 to about 7 Mt by 2050.
Meeting that growth would require output equivalent to 134 new lithium mines and more than $100bn of investment, according to Benchmark.
